Let \(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\) be an algebraic closure of \(\mathbb{Q}\), and let

\[
A=\{z\in \mathbb{C}: z \text{ is algebraic over } \mathbb{Q}\}
\]

be the field of algebraic numbers inside \(\mathbb{C}\). We count field homomorphisms

\[
f:\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\to \mathbb{C}
\]

that fix \(\mathbb{Q}\) pointwise.

### 1. The image must be \(A\)

Let \(f\) be such a homomorphism. Since \(f\) fixes \(1\), it is injective.

If \(\alpha\in \overline{\mathbb{Q}}\), then \(\alpha\) is algebraic over \(\mathbb{Q}\). Let \(m_\alpha(x)\in \mathbb{Q}[x]\) be its minimal polynomial. Then

\[
m_\alpha(f(\alpha))=f(m_\alpha(\alpha))=f(0)=0,
\]

so \(f(\alpha)\) is algebraic over \(\mathbb{Q}\). Hence

\[
f(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})\subseteq A.
\]

But \(f(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})\) is algebraically closed, because \(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\) is algebraically closed and \(f\) is an isomorphism onto its image. Also \(f(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})\) contains \(\mathbb{Q}\).

Now every element of \(A\) is algebraic over \(f(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})\), since it is algebraic over \(\mathbb{Q}\subseteq f(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})\). Because \(f(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})\) is algebraically closed, it must contain all of \(A\). Therefore

\[
f(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})=A.
\]

Thus the desired homomorphisms are exactly the \(\mathbb{Q}\)-automorphisms of \(A\):

\[
\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb{Q}}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}},\mathbb{C})
\cong
\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathbb{Q}}(A).
\]

### 2. Upper bound on the number

The field \(A=\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\) is countable, and \(\mathbb{C}\) has cardinality \(2^{\aleph_0}\). Therefore the set of all functions from \(A\) to \(\mathbb{C}\) has cardinality

\[
|\mathbb{C}|^{|A|}
=
(2^{\aleph_0})^{\aleph_0}
=
2^{\aleph_0}.
\]

So the number of such homomorphisms is at most \(2^{\aleph_0}\).

### 3. Lower bound: at least continuum many

For each prime \(p\), let \(\sqrt{p}\) be a square root in \(A\), and consider the field

\[
K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{p}: p \text{ prime})\subseteq A.
\]

For every subset \(S\) of the set of primes, define a map on \(K\) by

\[
\sigma_S(\sqrt{p})=
\begin{cases}
\sqrt{p}, & p\notin S,\\
-\sqrt{p}, & p\in S.
\end{cases}
\]

This is well-defined because the primes are independent modulo squares in \(\mathbb{Q}^\times\). On each finite subfield \(\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{p_1},\dots,\sqrt{p_n})\), this gives one of the \(2^n\) Galois automorphisms. Thus \(\sigma_S\) is a \(\mathbb{Q}\)-automorphism of \(K\).

Since \(A/\mathbb{Q}\) is normal and algebraic, every \(\mathbb{Q}\)-automorphism of \(K\) extends to a \(\mathbb{Q}\)-automorphism of \(A\). Distinct subsets \(S\) give distinct automorphisms, so there are at least

\[
2^{|\mathbb{P}|}=2^{\aleph_0}
\]

such homomorphisms.

Combining the upper and lower bounds, the number is exactly the cardinality of the continuum:

\[
\boxed{2^{\aleph_0}}
\]
